title: The Witness of the Fens
premise: Estate lawyer Sebastian Whitlock is summoned to the decaying Marsh House in the Fens to read the will of Edith Crane, a woman who vanished twelve years ago and was declared dead. Among her papers is a diary whose final entries continue past her disappearance, written in a hand Sebastian recognizes as belonging to his own late mentor—the man who taught him to keep the town's secrets filed and alphabetized. As the anniversary dinner approaches and the town's leading families close ranks, Sebastian follows the diary's clues through drained channels, drowned chapels, and falsified death certificates to find the witness everyone swears is dead: Edith herself, alive but memory-shattered, hidden by the very people who swore loyalty over truth. In the end Sebastian must choose between preserving the town's comfortable lies and exposing them at the anniversary dinner's raised glass, where he reads the true will aloud and shatters the silence that made him invisible.
about_author: Q. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing probate records in rural England before turning to fiction. Their novels are known for slow-burning mysteries steeped in landscape, paperwork, and the quiet violence of small-town memory.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Sebastian Whitlock receives a letter summoning him to Marsh House to execute a will for Edith Crane—declared dead twelve years ago. POV: Sebastian. The beat is unease: his carefully ordered life is cracked open by an impossible document bearing his mentor's notary seal.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Alphabetized Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present: Sebastian reflects on how he became keeper of the town's secrets after his mentor Aldous Fenwick's death, filing away what he saw the night Edith disappeared. POV: Sebastian. The emotional beat is guilt disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Marsh House at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Sebastian arrives at the flooded estate and meets the housekeeper, Mrs. Tallow, who claims Edith never existed beyond the missing-person file. POV: Sebastian. The beat is creeping isolation as the house itself seems to deny the past.

chapters.title: The Diary's Impossible Dates
chapters.summary: In the study safe, Sebastian finds Edith's diary; its entries continue three weeks past her disappearance, describing someone watching her from the reed beds. POV: Sebastian. The beat is vertigo—the first hard evidence that the town's story is a construction.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Committee
chapters.summary: Sebastian attends a planning meeting for the annual Founders' Dinner, where the town's patriarchs—Judge Harrow, Vicar Loomis, and brewer Cade—press him to finalize Edith's estate quietly. POV: Sebastian. The beat is polite menace beneath cassocks and cufflinks.

chapters.title: A Hand He Knew Too Well
chapters.summary: Forensic comparison confirms the post-disappearance diary entries were written by Aldous Fenwick, Sebastian's dead mentor. POV: Sebastian. The beat is betrayal—his father figure was either covering a murder or faking a death, and used Sebastian's own stationery.

chapters.title: What the Reeds Kept
chapters.summary: Following the diary's coordinates, Sebastian searches the drained fen channel and finds a child's shoe and a burnt hospital bracelet. POV: alternating with a brief interlude in Edith's fragmented diary voice. The beat is dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow's Second Story
chapters.summary: Confronted, the housekeeper admits she was paid for years by Judge Harrow to maintain the empty house—and that someone else has been living in the east wing. POV: Sebastian. The beat is the first crack of complicity breaking open.

chapters.title: The Witness Everyone Swears Is Dead
chapters.summary: In the sealed east wing, Sebastian finds Edith Crane alive, half-blind and memory-broken, tended by an anonymous caretaker who flees at his approach. POV: Sebastian. The beat is shock curdling into fury—who hid her, and why?

chapters.title: Loyalty, Filed Under F
chapters.summary: Edith, lucid in fragments, remembers trusting 'the kind one' the night she fled—but cannot name them. Sebastian realizes his mentor may have been her rescuer or her jailer. POV: Sebastian. The beat is grief for a hero unmade.

chapters.title: Harrow's Ledger
chapters.summary: Breaking into the judge's chambers, Sebastian finds ledgers showing payments to Fenwick and a second name redacted in every entry. POV: Sebastian. The beat is cold clarity: the conspiracy outlived its architect.

chapters.title: The Caretaker in the Chapel Ruins
chapters.summary: Sebastian traps the fleeing caretaker in the drowned chapel: it is Fenwick's daughter, Ruth, presumed lost abroad, who reveals her father hid Edith to protect her from the men at the dinner table. POV: Ruth, then Sebastian. The beat is two inheritances of secrecy colliding.

chapters.title: What Edith Saw
chapters.summary: Ruth produces Fenwick's confession letter: Edith witnessed a drowning at the Founders' Dinner twelve years ago—a boy, Cade's son—and the town chose the festival over the truth. POV: Sebastian reading aloud. The beat is horror at how ordinary the evil was.

chapters.title: The Boy in the Register
chapters.summary: Sebastian cross-checks parish registers and school rolls: the drowned boy was erased from every record, including files Sebastian himself archived without ever questioning. POV: Sebastian. The beat is self-indictment—he was the machine of forgetting.

chapters.title: An Invitation Refused
chapters.summary: Judge Harrow offers Sebastian partnership, a seat at the table, and the estate's fees if he certifies the will and burns the diary. POV: Sebastian. The beat is temptation rendered almost reasonable—the exact choice his mentor refused.

chapters.title: Memory Returns on the Rising Tide
chapters.summary: Walking Edith along the fen at high water, a bell from the chapel triggers her memory: she names the men who watched the boy drown and did nothing. POV: Edith, her first full chapter. The beat is a shattered woman reclaiming herself as witness.

chapters.title: Tallow's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tallow breaks down: she is the boy's aunt, paid into silence, and gives Sebastian the last piece—photographs from the dinner night. POV: Sebastian. The beat is sorrow for the many small betrayals that built one large lie.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Glass Is Raised
chapters.summary: Sebastian drafts the true will, copies the evidence, and sends letters to every family, knowing there is no way back. Ruth begs him to run; he refuses. POV: Sebastian. The beat is terrified resolve—invisibility finally surrendered.

chapters.title: The Founders' Dinner
chapters.summary: At the anniversary dinner, glasses rise to the town's founders while Harrow watches Sebastian for signs of compliance. POV: Sebastian. The beat is suffocating suspense as the toast begins.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Instead of the false will, Sebastian reads Edith's testimony and names the drowned boy; Edith herself enters the hall, alive, and the room fractures—Cade collapses, Loomis prays, Harrow reaches for the ledger. POV: Sebastian. The beat is cathartic detonation.

chapters.title: Aftermath in the Drained Light
chapters.summary: Harrow is arrested; Cade confesses to the cover-up; the town must live with its exhumed history. Edith, restored to her own name, asks Sebastian why he came. POV: Sebastian. The beat is exhausted, unsentimental justice.

chapters.title: The Witness of the Fens
chapters.summary: Months later, Sebastian closes his old archive and opens a new file labeled with the boy's real name, keeping memory instead of secrets. Edith visits Marsh House as its owner at last. POV: Sebastian. The beat is quiet redemption: truth kept, loyalty redefined.
